newsitem.title: USA: Clinton intervenes to stop American Airlines strike.
newsitem.headline: Clinton intervenes to stop American Airlines strike.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday intervened to avert a strike by American Airlines pilots, appointing a presidential board to study the dispute and postponing a walkout at the second-largest U.S. carrier for 60 days.

"To facilitate an agreement, and because I believe that a strike would have an immediate and adverse impact on the traveling public, I am creating a Presidential Emergency Board to work with the parties and to make recommendations regarding a resolution," Clinton said in a statement.
"No strike will occur while the ... board is in place."

Acting minutes after 12:01 a.m. EST (0501 GMT), when the pilots announced they were on strike, Clinton invoked his power under the Railway Labor Act to name the board, which must make non-binding recommendations within 30 days.

American, a unit of Fort Worth-based AMR Corp., and the Allied Pilots' Association union will then have a further 30 days to act on the board's recommendations, reach their own settlement or resort to "self-help," meaning a lockout by the company or a strike by the union, U.S. officials said.

The strike threat had already caused major disruption to the U.S. air travel system, sending many passengers scrambling to change their bookings from American ahead of the three-day Presidents Day holiday weekend.

But a strike itself could have proved far more costly, shutting down the airline, which carries 20 percent of the nation's air travelers, and costing the economy up to an estimated $200 million a day.
American, which has 2,200 flights carrying about 200,000 passengers a day, had canceled most international flights and a few of its domestic flights in anticipation of a strike.

American's President Donald Carty said he was relieved the airline would continue to operate, but disappointed the pilots had not accepted the final offer extended to them on Friday via the federal mediator overseeing the talks since Monday.
"We're very disappointed," Carty said. "If there is any silver lining to the cloud, the airline is operating. We're delighted that it's operating."

Carty, who estimated the net loss to American Airlines from the run-up to the strike at $100 million, said the two sides had been close in their negotiating stances. "The issue was pure money ... just pure raw economics."
James Sovich, the pilots union president who announced the decision to strike, said the negotiations had been "tedious and frustrating," adding: "Our decision to cease operations is a painful one."
Sovich later told a news conference that the strike had lasted 24 minutes, saying the union was officially notified of the president's decision at 12:25 a.m. EST (0525 GMT).

Travel agents said a strike would have battered the tourist industry in the Caribbean, which is in its peak winter holiday season, and caused havoc as well at major airports in Chicago, Miami, New York, Los Angeles and other cities.
The key issues in the talks were pay for pilots flying big jets and whether members of the union should fly smaller jets for American's commuter carrier, American Eagle.
American has said it needs to fly the new, small jets with lower-paid pilots from another union if it is to compete with other major carriers offering low-cost commuter flights.

Brian Mayhew, the pilots' chief negotiator, said on Thursday that the pilots had offered a new proposal on pay -- presumably less than the 11.5 percent pay increase over four years sought earlier -- but gave no details. The latest offer from American was a 6 percent raise over four years.
The stock of AMR Corp., American's parent, fell $1.25 to $81.875 on the New York Stock Exchange on Friday.
